P-multiregion-ledger.flaw: Cross-region settlement forces the US region to hold/transmit an EU counterparty's account id and amount (GDPR personal data); treating it as non-personal violates data-residency constraint 4.

Summing per-region EOD snapshots taken at independent HLC watermarks is not a globally consistent cut, so in-flight cross-region transfers are double-counted or dropped (and suspense cannot close while the link is down).

During the 30+ min partition cross-region transfers cannot complete (sender debited to suspense, payee uncreditable), stranding regulated funds; the rec wrongly treats in-region writability as sufficient.
The cross-region saga specifies no idempotency/dedup key, so a transfer-intent re-emitted after the partition heals can double-credit the destination.
Saga compensation has no failure handling (no timeout/dead-letter/repair loop), so a failed reversal or partial credit strands customer funds in suspense indefinitely.

Exactly-once outbox sagas, suspense accounting, signed-watermark snapshots and reconciliation are substantial distributed-systems work; feasibility is asserted, not demonstrated, for a 6-person team with no multi-region experience in 9 months.

P-feature-store-skew.flaw: Point-in-time backfill across years (constraint 2) is impossible for new online-only features because logs only exist from when logging was turned on, so logged-features-as-training-data cannot reproduce historical values.
The GDPR 30-day deletion design omits the new feature-log Kafka topic and the materialized training vectors derived from it, which contain entity-keyed PII.
'Codegen from one DSL means it cannot drift' is false — Flink and Spark differ in windowing/watermarking/late-data/numeric behavior; only a replay-equality test catches the skew.
Logging the full served feature vector at serving QPS is a large net storage/compute increase against an already-70%-consumed budget, and the rec never shows it fits.

Using only logged features for the candidates the live model served is selection bias with zero counterfactual coverage, leaving a new model that scores un-served candidates without training features.

The train/serve consistency test checks value equality but not null/coverage skew (an online KV miss returns a default while offline has a real value), a leading cause of offline-strong/online-weak gaps.

P-zero-downtime-shard.flaw: App-level dual-write across old MySQL and the new shard is not atomic, so a crash/partial failure drops or duplicates events (violating constraint 1); idempotent keys only dedupe retries, and binlog/CDC is the actual no-loss mechanism while reconciliation only detects drift after the fact.

Sub-sharding the 18% mega-tenant destroys its single-shard locality, turning its dashboards into cross-shard scatter-gather and putting the largest tenant's sub-2s SLA most at risk; isolating it also contradicts hash-to-vbucket routing and needs an undefined directory/override layer.

ProxySQL tenant_id routing only works for queries carrying a tenant_id predicate; legacy queries without it, cross-tenant JOINs, global AUTO_INCREMENT dependencies, and admin/background/multi-tenant jobs break, so the rewrite budget is underestimated.
The cross-tenant sub-2s aggregate store introduces ingestion lag and a consistency gap versus the sharded source that is never reconciled.
Continuing to dual-write to the already-saturated old DB plus adding continuous reconciliation reads against it increases load on the failing system throughout the months-long migration.
Reversibility is only argued for the read-flip phase; the irreversible write-authority cutover and its rollback are never described, so 'reversible at any point' is overclaimed.

P-autoscale-stampede.flaw: Single-flight does not prevent the fleet-wide DB stampede — across instances each repopulates the same cold key without a distributed lock, and a surge to many distinct cold keys isn't coalesced at all.
A hard PgBouncer cap relocates the bottleneck to an unbounded pooler queue, so under 10x the latency cascade reappears as queueing unless the queue is explicitly bounded with fast-fail/edge limits.
PgBouncer transaction mode breaks session-scoped features (prepared statements, advisory locks, session SETs/state), a compatibility risk asserted without verification.
Routing core reads to replicas during a 10x surge introduces replication-lag staleness, conflicting with constraint 5's prohibition on dangerously stale reads on write-sensitive paths.
With a 45s cold start, absorbing an unscheduled 10x-in-60s spike requires a warm pool near surge capacity, i.e. the sustained over-provisioning cost constraint 2 forbids — the worst case is unsolved.
Fail-closed/load-shedding on write-sensitive endpoints conflicts with constraint 6 (core read paths must stay available) where those paths are core, and the conflict is unresolved.

P-churn-winback.flaw: A retention-only save/pause flow with no expansion lever cannot push NRR above 100% (the board target requires net expansion), so it commits to the target with a mechanism that structurally cannot reach it.
The primary metric (incremental net revenue at 6 months) reads out after Q3 and after the year-end NRR deadline, so it cannot inform the decision within the window.
The design exceeds the 'engineering can fully resource only one' constraint by bundling cancel-screen segmentation + a downgrade tier + a re-engagement nudge + a re-onboarding push.
The pause flow risks negative near-term revenue and cannibalization (pausers pay $0, and full-price retainers get diverted into pausing), and the net effect is not established.
The pause flow only intercepts at the cancel screen and does nothing about the upstream rise in churn from 2.4% to 3.1%.

P-warehouse-siting.flaw: The justification is logically inverted: linehaul-dominated freight means cost/time scale with distance, so a closer Southeast/Atlanta node shortens the dominant leg and argues FOR a second node, not against it.
Re-slotting and carrier-zone renegotiation cannot shorten the physical Columbus-to-SE/TX linehaul transit, so option (c) structurally may not recover the 2-day promise if the miss is distance-driven.
The diagnosis that the miss is 'carrier-zone/slotting before distance' is asserted without evidence and contradicts the misses clustering in the farthest regions.

The trigger to start building 12 months before breakeven volume reintroduces the ahead-of-demand betting the rec criticizes, and forecasting a small-base 25%-YoY threshold 12 months out is highly uncertain (fires early or late, with unquantified lost-sales/brand cost).

P-pricing-migration.flaw: A single project allotment cannot cleanly separate SMBs from whales on a projects-per-seat continuum: project-heavy SMBs are over-charged (churn risk) while seat-heavy whales slip under the threshold.
Billing whales on variable active-project usage makes the pitched incremental/growth revenue usage-variable, undercutting the predictability finance needs for the raise.
The 'active projects' meter is gameable (customers archive/close/reopen projects) and the 'active' definition is ambiguous/dispute-prone, eroding the targeted whale revenue.

Because migration is renewal-gated and annual seat contracts run up to 11 months, most whales aren't migrated within the two-quarter window, so the success metric is unobservable and leakage persists past the decision point.
'Active projects' is never shown to track the actual infra cost driver (top 8% = 55% of cost); if cost is storage/compute/events rather than project count, metering projects won't recover it.
The sequencing is internally inconsistent: 'launch the hybrid for new accounts immediately' conflicts with 'fix sales comp first,' a multi-month change.

P-capex-automation.flaw: The EV/EBITDA claim is wrong: debt paydown is computed below EBITDA so it doesn't change EBITDA (a buyer on EV/EBITDA sees it unchanged), whereas high-margin growth revenue is the multiple-accretive lever — the 'EBITDA-to-a-buyer story' is mis-stated.

The rec names customer concentration as the binding risk but fails to reduce it — it rejects (b), the option that diversifies away from the 38% anchor, and its chosen pilot still depends on that anchor renewing, lowering dollars-at-risk but not concentration.
A 'smaller pilot that scales without re-buying' may not exist: molding-automation cells have a minimum viable scale, so a half-scale pilot may be uneconomic and fail to validate cell economics.
Splitting the $8M across debt paydown and a pilot risks doing neither at needle-moving scale (sub-scale on both).
Calling debt paydown a 'guaranteed risk-free return equal to the borrowing rate' overstates it, since interest is tax-deductible so the real return is ~rate*(1-tax).
